_comment: How Japanese's phrases hold together, for lib/chunker.py.
_np_head: 赤い花, 大きな家: the modifier comes first and attaches forward to the noun it modifies.
_adposition: Japanese has postpositions, and they are written as particles: 山へ, 学校に, 漢字を. A particle closes the phrase it follows -- which is the bunsetsu, and the unit this language is read in.
_min: a bunsetsu may be one dictionary word plus its particles, and the tokens here are dictionary words, so one is a real chunk.
_words: WITH SUDACHIPY INSTALLED (lib/words.py) A SENTENCE IS NOT READ OFF ITS CHARACTERS AT ALL. It is cut between the words the word strip shows, by the part of speech SudachiPy names for each: a particle, an auxiliary, a suffix and a mark stay with what they follow; a modifier binds forward (この, 大きな, the attributive 元気な and 流れてきた, and の); a noun keeps the する that makes it a verb; は and も are FIRM, が too unless its verb comes next, and every other particle leans toward the verb after it -- and then the pieces grow to grow_to, below. So a chunk cannot end inside a word, which is exactly what the characters cannot promise: 冷たい雨が、窓の外にながれ落ちる。 was once cut 冷たい雨が、窓の外になが | れ落ちる。, max_chars reading the が of ながれ as a particle. Everything from here down is what a Python without the analyzer reads instead.
_marks: PUNCTUATION ENDS A CLAUSE, and a clause boundary is a chunk boundary. A mark cuts whatever follows it, kana included (柴刈りに、| おばあさんは), and it is read BEFORE the particles. Without it a particle before a comma was a particle refused, because 、 is not a content word: 寒い朝に、窓を開ける。 came out 寒い朝に、窓を | 開ける。 -- its one cut the を before a kanji -- and 冷たい雨が、窓の外にながれ落ちる。 ran on to max_chars and was cut inside ながれ. A quote or bracket closing on a mark stays with it and cuts only before a content word, because Japanese quotes into a particle: 「待ってくれ！」と彼は. The ASCII full stop and comma are not here: in Japanese text they are a decimal point or a list of figures far more often than a clause.
_closes:
A bunsetsu ends after its particles, and that is the whole of how Japanese is read. These are checked against the CHARACTERS and not against the dictionary's word list: longest match is greedy and reads へし as a verb and ています as a noun, so a cut that trusted it inherited both mistakes. Longest particles first, so から is not read as ら after か.
の IS NOT HERE. It is the genitive and the attributive, and this toolbox's own rule is that a modifier is never split from its noun (私の本, 赤い花) -- so の binds forward like an ezafe rather than closing anything. Listing it cut この into この | 問題, which is a determiner torn off the noun it determines.
て IS HERE because a chunk ends after a verb form as well as after a particle, and the te-form is where a Japanese sentence joins one clause to the next. It is safe only BECAUSE of the content-word rule above: して詳しく cuts (詳 is kanji) and しています does not (い is kana), which is exactly the difference between a clause seam and a verb with its auxiliary.
_firm: The particles after which a piece stays apart when the pieces grow: the topic, the subject, and a clause joined to the next. おじいさんは | 山へ柴刈りに, not おじいさんは山へ. The one exception is the sentence's last piece, its verb as a rule, which may still join what it follows: 雨が | 降る。 is too small a pair to be two chunks, and comes out 雨が降る。
_opens_content: A particle only ENDS a phrase when a new content word begins after it -- kanji, katakana, a latin word, a number. Followed by more hiragana it is far more likely to be inside a word or a verb ending (して, には) than to be closing anything.
_max_chars: A run of hiragana with no content word in it gives the rule above nothing to cut before -- an all-kana sentence came out whole. Past this many characters a particle may close a phrase anyway: a long chunk is a worse answer than a slightly early one.
_grow_to: How many characters (the punctuation not counted) two neighbouring pieces may come to and still be joined into one chunk: the 2-8 docs/lang/ja.md asks for. Cut after every particle, a sentence falls apart into a word and its particle at a time -- 本を | 読んで | 映画を | 見ました -- which is a dictionary entry, not a phrase. Grown while they fit, the weakest seam first, an object keeps its verb: 本を読んで | 映画を見ました, 窓を開ける。 Nothing is ever joined across a mark.
